claims.claim: 18 nucleotides of homology (above 45°C annealing temperature) and 2 hr of 3Cs reaction time were sufficient for 3Cs reactions.
claims.source: To gain insights into the oligonucleotide requirements and kinetics of 3Cs reactions, we tested different 3Cs homology lengths of 10, 13, 15, and 18 nucleotides, performed a 3Cs reaction time series, and demonstrated that 18 nucleotides of homology (above 45°C annealing temperature) and 2 hr of 3Cs reaction time were sufficient (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–C) (Kunkel, 2001).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated experimentally in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–C.

claims.claim: 81% of pLentiGuide and 82% of plentiCRISPRv2 bacterial clones contained GFP-targeting gRNAs after 3Cs synthesis.
claims.source: Bacterial clones were grown and their plasmid DNA Sanger sequenced, revealing that 81% of pLentiGuide and 82% of plentiCRISPRv2 contained GFP-targeting gRNAs (Figure 1D and Figure 1—figure supplement 1D).
claims.evidence: This is determined by Sanger sequencing of individual clones.

claims.claim: I-SceI-mediated removal of wildtype plasmids reduced their level to below the detection limit.
claims.source: Although the effect of increased dU concentrations was negligible, I-SceI-mediated removal of wildtype plasmids reduced their level to below our detection limit (Figure 1D and Figure 1—figure supplement 1D–F).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by NGS data showing <0.3% wildtype remnants after I-SceI digest.

claims.claim: The plentiCRISPRv2 GFP library had an average read count of 1.15 million per GFP sequence with a wildtype rate below 0.3%.
claims.source: We performed next-generation sequencing (NGS) on the plentiCRISPRv2 sample with an average read count of 1.15 million per GFP sequence and identified a wildtype rate of below 0.3% in the absence of any apparent sequence bias (Figure 1E and Supplementary file 1).
claims.evidence: This is determined by NGS analysis.

claims.claim: A one-sided Chi-squared test for goodness of fit identified a uniform distribution (p=0.1) of all six GFP gRNA sequences.
claims.source: A one-sided Chi-squared test for goodness of fit identified a uniform distribution (p=0.1) of all six gRNA sequences.
claims.evidence: This is a statistical test performed on the NGS data.

claims.claim: The GFP library had a coefficient of variation of 33.18% and an area under the curve of 0.56.
claims.source: The uniform gRNA distribution was supported by a low coefficient of variation (CV) of 33.18% and an area under the curve (AUC, Lorenz curve) of only 0.56 (Figure 1E–F and Figure 1—figure supplement 1G).
claims.evidence: These metrics are calculated from the NGS data to assess distribution uniformity.

claims.claim: 3Cs gRNAs induced robust GFP gene editing as demonstrated by T7 Endonuclease I assay.
claims.source: Seven days post-transduction, we performed a T7 Endonuclease I assay and observed robust GFP gene editing, both by a single GFP-targeting 3Cs gRNA (3Cs-gRNA) and by the pool of six 3Cs-gRNAs, whereas un-transduced (–) and an NHT control gRNA failed to edit the GFP gene (Figure 1G).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by the T7 endonuclease assay shown in Figure 1G.

claims.claim: GFP gene editing by 3Cs gRNAs translated to a lentiviral dose-dependent loss of GFP protein.
claims.source: GFP gene editing translated to a lentiviral dose-dependent loss of GFP protein when analyzed by fluorescence flow-cytometry and immunoblotting (Figure 1H–I and Figure 1—figure supplement 1H).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by flow cytometry and immunoblotting data in Figure 1H-I.

claims.claim: The 3Cs technology enables the rapid and cloning-free generation of high-quality single and pooled CRISPR/Cas gRNAs.
claims.source: Taken together, we demonstrate that the 3Cs technology enables the rapid and cloning-free generation of high-quality single and pooled CRISPR/Cas gRNAs.
claims.evidence: This conclusion is supported by all the GFP targeting experiments.

claims.claim: Six degenerated 3Cs oligonucleotides with increasing numbers of randomized nucleotides were designed to mimic gRNA sequence pools with diversities ranging from 256 to 262,144 individual sequences.
claims.source: To test this hypothesis, we designed six degenerated 3Cs oligonucleotides with increasing numbers of randomized nucleotides to mimic gRNA sequence pools with diversities ranging from 256 to 262,144 individual sequences (Figure 2A).
claims.evidence: This is described in the text and shown in Figure 2A.

claims.claim: NGS and computational analyses identified all individual sequences in the randomized libraries with uniform distributions (AUC values between 0.6 and 0.73).
claims.source: Independent of an oligonucleotide's diversity, NGS and computational analyses identified all of the individual sequences and uniform distributions with area under the curve values between 0.6 and 0.73 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B and Supplementary file 2).
claims.evidence: This is determined by NGS analysis and shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claims.claim: A prominent cytosine bias was observed in the randomized libraries, with C contents above 40% within the top 10% of the most abundant gRNAs.
claims.source: Despite the uniform distribution, we observed a prominent cytosine (C) bias in the randomized libraries, with C contents of above 40% within the top 10% of the most abundant gRNAs (Figure 2C).
claims.evidence: This is shown in Figure 2C by plotting gRNA abundance versus C content.

claims.claim: The C bias is probably due to incomplete phosphoramidite mixing during oligonucleotide synthesis.
claims.source: We reasoned that the C bias is probably due to incomplete phosphoramidite mixing during oligonucleotide synthesis and should therefore be absent from gRNA libraries containing nonrandom gRNA sequences (Ellington and Pollard, 2009).
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on known issues with oligonucleotide synthesis and supported by a citation.

claims.claim: The nonrandom DUB library was absent of C bias.
claims.source: To test this hypothesis, we designed and generated a nonrandom 3Cs-gRNA library targeting all 105 human DUBs, each with three gRNAs (DUB library). NGS and nucleotide content analysis confirmed our hypothesis and revealed the absence of C bias from the nonrandom DUB library (Figure 2C and Supplementary file 3).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by NGS analysis shown in Figure 2C.

claims.claim: Normalizing read counts using individual nucleotide frequencies led to improved AUC values and sequence distributions.
claims.source: To correct the randomized libraries for the C bias, we determined the individual nucleotide frequency at every randomized position and used these frequencies to normalize the original read counts, leading to improved AUC values and sequence distributions (Figure 2D and Supplementary file 2) and further confirming the uncoupling of sequence diversity and distribution in 3Cs reactions.
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by the improved Lorenz curves in Figure 2D.

claims.claim: 3Cs is a robust technology that uncouples sequence distribution from sequence diversity.
claims.source: Taken together, these findings lead us to conclude that 3Cs is a robust technology that uncouples sequence distribution from sequence diversity and, therefore, is a powerful alternative technology to conventional gRNA cloning methods for generating gRNA libraries.
claims.evidence: This conclusion is supported by the data from libraries with varying diversities all showing uniform distributions.

claims.claim: The DUB proliferation screen was performed in biological duplicates with an MOI of 0.2 and library coverage of 1,000.
claims.source: Next, we investigated the performance of 3Cs-gRNA reagents in cellular screenings. To do so, we generated infectious lentiviral particles of the 3Cs-gRNA DUB library and applied them to a proliferation screen in non-transformed hTERT–RPE1 cells in biological duplicates (multiplicity of infection (MOI) 0.2, coverage 1,000).
claims.evidence: This describes the experimental design of the DUB screen.

claims.claim: R2 values of 0.95, 0.88, and 0.90 were determined for time points day 0, 11, and 21, respectively, in the DUB screen.
claims.source: In line with reports of the high experimental reproducibility of CRISPR/Cas screenings (Evers et al., 2016; Morgens et al., 2016), we determined R2 values of 0.95, 0.88, and 0.90 for time points day 0, 11, and 21, respectively (Figure 3—figure supplement 3A–C).
claims.evidence: These correlation values are calculated from biological replicates and shown in supplementary figures.

claims.claim: Spearman correlation and Shapiro–Wilk confidence tests revealed correlations above 0.88 and p-values below 0.001 in the DUB screen.
claims.source: Spearman correlation and Shapiro–Wilk confidence tests revealed correlations of above 0.88 and p-values of below 0.001, respectively, demonstrating a high experimental confidence in the level of gRNA representation (Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 3A–C) (Shapiro and Wilk, 1965).
claims.evidence: These statistical tests are performed on the replicate data.

claims.claim: PSMD14, USP7 and COPS6 are positive regulators of hTERT–RPE1 proliferation.

claims.evidence: This is inferred from the negative proliferation phenotype upon depletion.

claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to prior screening studies.

claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to recent work on p53-mediated effects.

claims.claim: A trend of increased phenotype resolution among negative gene ranks over time was observed.
claims.source: Indeed, when comparing normalized gene ranks, we observed a trend of increased phenotype resolution among negative gene ranks over time, although this effect was largely absent from positive gene ranks (Figure 3—figure supplement 1I and Figure 3—figure supplement 2 and 3).

claims.source: Depletion of USP28 and USP46 induced the strongest positive change, whereas deletion of USP22, USP48 or TNFAIP3 induced the most significant negative change, in phenotype between day 11 and day 21, suggesting a time-dependent absence of compensatory mechanisms to accommodate an early loss-of-function phenotype (Figure 3E–F and Figure 3—figure supplement 3I).

claims.claim: Time-dependent phenotype changes suggest a time-dependent absence of compensatory mechanisms to accommodate an early loss-of-function phenotype.
claims.source: Depletion of USP28 and USP46 induced the strongest positive change, whereas deletion of USP22, USP48 or TNFAIP3 induced the most significant negative change, in phenotype between day 11 and day 21, suggesting a time-dependent absence of compensatory mechanisms to accommodate an early loss-of-function phenotype (Figure 3E–F and Figure 3—figure supplement 3I).
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation of the time-dependent phenotype data.

claims.claim: Depletion of USP28 and BRCC3 induced a rapid positive proliferation effect as validated by shRNA.
claims.source: When compared to negative- (Luciferase) and positive-control (Plk1) shRNA sequences, depletion of USP28 and BRCC3 induced a rapid positive proliferation effect (Figure 3G).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by the validation experiment shown in Figure 3G.

claims.claim: Depletion of USP7 and COPS6 induced an instant and strong negative proliferation effect as validated by shRNA.
claims.source: By contrast, depletion of USP7 and COPS6 induced an instant and strong negative proliferation effect (Figure 3G), validating the gRNA-mediated knockout phenotypes.
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by the validation experiment shown in Figure 3G.

claims.claim: The shRNA validation experiments validate the gRNA-mediated knockout phenotypes.
claims.source: By contrast, depletion of USP7 and COPS6 induced an instant and strong negative proliferation effect (Figure 3G), validating the gRNA-mediated knockout phenotypes.
claims.evidence: The shRNA results are consistent with the gRNA screen results.

claims.claim: The analysis demonstrates the quality and fidelity of 3Cs reagents in functional genomics applications.
claims.source: Collectively, our analysis demonstrates the quality and fidelity of 3Cs reagents in functional genomics applications.
claims.evidence: This conclusion is supported by the DUB screen and validation data.

claims.claim: CRISPR/Cas technology has become the method of choice for gene perturbation experiments.
claims.source: Owing to its versatility,CRISPR/Cas technology has become the method of choice for gene perturbation experiments, yet classical short hairpin RNAs (shRNA, RNAi) are still widely used.
claims.evidence: This is a general statement about the field supported by common knowledge.

claims.claim: shRNA oligonucleotides contain complementary sequences that form stable secondary structures that render the generation of shRNA reagents inefficient.
claims.source: However, shRNA oligonucleotides contain complementary sequences that form stable secondary structures that render the generation of shRNA reagents inefficient (McIntyre and Fanning, 2006).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work on shRNA synthesis challenges.

claims.claim: The denaturation and annealing step in 3Cs circumvents the secondary structures of shRNA oligonucleotides.
claims.source: A crucial step in our improved Kunkel mutagenesis technology is the denaturation of the gRNA-encoding oligonucleotides and their subsequent annealing to template ssDNA (see 'Materials and methods' section). Owing to this denaturation and annealing step, we anticipated that improved Kunkel mutagenesis would circumvent the secondary structures of shRNA oligonucleotide and enable the generation of shRNA reagents.
claims.evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the protocol design.

claims.claim: 3Cs reactions using 60 ng and 120 ng of ssDNA yielded the characteristic 3Cs-DNA band pattern with no major difference in bacterial transformation efficiency.
claims.source: We performed two parallel 3Cs reactions using 60 ng and 120 ng of ssDNA, and both reactions yielded the characteristic 3Cs-DNA band pattern with no major difference in bacterial transformation efficiency between the two tested scales (Figure 3—figure supplement 2C).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by gel electrophoresis in Figure 3—figure supplement 2C.

claims.claim: SANGER sequencing confirmed the successful integration of the GFP–shRNA sequence into pLKO.1.
claims.source: To demonstrate the successful integration of the GFP–shRNA sequence into pLKO.1, we amplified single bacterial clones carrying 3Cs-DNA of shRNA reactions and analyzed their plasmid DNA by SANGER sequencing. This resulted in the expected GFP–shRNA sequence and the absence of adjacent nucleotide changes (Figure 3—figure supplement 2D), from which we concluded that 3Cs is a versatile technology that generates high-quality gRNA and shRNA reagents.
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by Sanger sequencing shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2D.

claims.claim: 3Cs is a versatile technology that generates high-quality gRNA and shRNA reagents.
claims.source: To demonstrate the successful integration of the GFP–shRNA sequence into pLKO.1, we amplified single bacterial clones carrying 3Cs-DNA of shRNA reactions and analyzed their plasmid DNA by SANGER sequencing. This resulted in the expected GFP–shRNA sequence and the absence of adjacent nucleotide changes (Figure 3—figure supplement 2D), from which we concluded that 3Cs is a versatile technology that generates high-quality gRNA and shRNA reagents.
claims.evidence: This conclusion is supported by successful generation of both gRNA and shRNA reagents.

claims.claim: GFP-targeting 3Cs-shRNA reduced GFP-fluorescence by more than 60% in transduced cells.
claims.source: To demonstrate 3Cs-shRNA fidelity, we generated infectious lentiviral particles of the GFP-targeting 3Cs-shRNA and transduced GFP-positive hTERT–RPE1 cells. Strikingly, 96 hr after lentiviral transduction, we observed a reduction in GFP-fluorescence, confirming the functionality of the 3Cs-shRNAs in cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 2E).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by flow cytometry in Figure 3—figure supplement 2E.

claims.claim: The E2 3Cs-shRNA library had a wildtype remnant level of 0.04%, a CV of 37.9% and an AUC of 0.68.
claims.source: To determine the E2 3Cs-shRNA distribution more accurately, we performed NGS sequencing with an average shRNA read count of >8,300 and determined a wildtype remnant level of 0.04%, a CV of 37.9% and an AUC of 0.68, demonstrating an almost uniform distribution (Figure 3—figure supplement 3D–E).
claims.evidence: These metrics are calculated from NGS data.

claims.claim: The Bsu36I digest does not affect 3Cs-shRNA sequence distribution.
claims.source: To correlate 3Cs-shRNA abundance and the distribution of the E2 3Cs-shRNA libraries before and after Bsu36I enzyme digest, we determined the ratios of their respective normalized read counts. Importantly, all ratios were close to one and lined up close to the respective diagonal with a linear regression R2 of 0.9687 (Figure 3—figure supplement 5F), demonstrating a high correlation of individual data points and no influence of the Bsu36I digest on 3Cs-shRNA sequence distribution.
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by comparing distributions before and after digest in Figure 3—figure supplement 5F.

claims.claim: The 3Cs technology can be adapted to generate high-quality shRNA reagents in single and pooled formats.
claims.source: In summary, this demonstrates that our 3Cs technology can be adapted to generate high-quality shRNA reagents in single and pooled formats.
claims.evidence: This conclusion is supported by the successful generation of single and pooled shRNA libraries.

claims.claim: 3Cs gRNA library diversity is mostly limited by the number of distinguishable oligonucleotides within a 3Cs reaction and the subsequent bacterial electroporation efficiencies.
claims.source: Thus, we hypothesized that 3Cs gRNA library diversity is mostly limited by the number of distinguishable oligonucleotides within a 3Cs reaction and the subsequent bacterial electroporation efficiencies.
claims.evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the technical aspects of the method.

claims.claim: Limitations in electroporation efficiencies can be overcome by accumulating the individual efficiencies of multiple parallel reactions.
claims.source: Limitations in electroporation efficiencies can be overcome by accumulating the individual efficiencies of multiple parallel reactions, as routinely performed to amplify phage libraries with diversities beyond 109 (Smith and Scott, 1993).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work on phage library amplification.

claims.claim: The number of distinguishable oligonucleotides is limited by the capacity of synthetic oligonucleotide synthesis.
claims.source: The number of distinguishable oligonucleotides is limited by the capacity of synthetic oligonucleotide synthesis, rendering truly genome-wide gene perturbation libraries unfeasible.
claims.evidence: This is a statement about the technical limitations of oligonucleotide synthesis.

claims.claim: A cumulative transformation efficiency of 1.2 × 10^10 was achieved for the TGW library, accounting for ~16% of TGW sequences.
claims.source: Importantly, we note that the amplification of this degenerated library is limited by the number of transformed bacteria. As complete generation of this reagent is currently unfeasible, we limited our efforts to eight parallel electroporation reactions and achieved a cumulative transformation efficiency of 1.2 × 1010, accounting for ~16% of TGW sequences, assuming a stringent uniform sequence distribution.
claims.evidence: This is a measured transformation efficiency from the experimental protocol.

claims.claim: 94.19% of TGW NGS reads were unique.
claims.source: In order to approximate the gRNA distribution, we generated 14.4 million NGS reads and found 94.19% to be unique (Figure 4C and Supplementary file 9).
claims.evidence: This is determined by NGS analysis shown in Figure 4C.

claims.claim: The nucleotide frequencies extracted from TGW NGS reads matched the initially applied degenerated oligonucleotide sequence.
claims.source: We went on to extract the nucleotide frequencies for each gRNA position from TGW NGS reads, translated them to IUPAC nomenclature, and identified the identical degenerated sequence that we initially applied in the form of the degenerated oligonucleotide pool (Figure 4D).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by the nucleotide frequency analysis in Figure 4D.

claims.claim: The TGW library had a CV of 0.26% and an AUC of 0.52, suggesting a nearly uniform distribution.
claims.source: Furthermore, the distribution of TGW read counts had a CV of 0.26% and an AUC of 0.52, suggesting a nearly uniform distribution of sequenced and represented gRNA sequences (Figure 4E–F) (Makowski and Soares, 2003).
claims.evidence: These metrics are calculated from NGS data and shown in Figure 4E-F.

claims.claim: Doxorubicin induces a robust, irreversible and dose-dependent reduction of cell viability in hTERT–RPE1 cells within 4 days.

claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by the dose-response curve in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A.

claims.claim: The validation screen reidentified 2,716 gRNAs of which 795 were more than two-fold enriched after 21 d of doxorubicin treatment.

results.result: The 3Cs technology successfully generates high-quality CRISPR/Cas gRNA libraries with uniform distribution that uncouples sequence diversity from sequence distribution. The method converts lentiviral plasmids to dU-containing circular ssDNA, achieves >80% correct gRNA integration, reduces wildtype remnants to <0.3%, and produces functional gRNAs that induce dose-dependent gene editing.
results.evaluation: Claims C29-C40 provide converging experimental evidence from gel electrophoresis (C29-C30), Sanger sequencing (C33), NGS analysis (C35-C37), statistical testing (C36), and functional assays (C38-C39). The chi-squared test (p=0.1, C36), low CV (33.18%, C37), and AUC (0.56, C37) demonstrate uniform distribution. T7 endonuclease and flow cytometry data (C38-C39) confirm functional gene editing. The I-SceI digest effectively removes wildtype remnants (<0.3%, C34-C35).

results.result: 3Cs technology maintains uniform gRNA distribution (AUC 0.6-0.73) across libraries with diversities ranging from 256 to 262,144 sequences, demonstrating uncoupling of sequence diversity from distribution. A cytosine bias was observed in randomized libraries but absent in non-random libraries, and could be computationally corrected.
results.evaluation: Claims C41-C42 demonstrate uniform distribution across six libraries with increasing diversity through NGS analysis. The cytosine bias observation (C43) is mechanistically explained by incomplete phosphoramidite mixing (C44), validated by its absence in the non-random DUB library (C45), and successfully corrected computationally (C46). This provides strong evidence for the core claim that 3Cs uncouples diversity from distribution (C47).

results.result: The DUB proliferation screen using 3Cs gRNA libraries demonstrated high fidelity and reproducibility (R² 0.88-0.95, Spearman >0.88), identified USP28 and BRCC3 as negative regulators and PSMD14, USP7, and COPS6 as positive regulators of hTERT-RPE1 proliferation, with validation by shRNA confirming the phenotypes.
results.evaluation: The screen design (C48) with appropriate MOI (0.2) and coverage (1,000) shows high reproducibility across biological replicates (C49-C50). MAGeCK analysis identified consistent phenotypes at multiple timepoints (C51-C54), and independent shRNA validation (C63-C65) confirms the gRNA-mediated phenotypes. Time-dependent analysis (C58, C60-C62) provides additional mechanistic insights. The convergence of multiple lines of evidence strongly supports the fidelity of 3Cs reagents (C66).

results.result: The 3Cs technology was successfully adapted to generate high-quality shRNA reagents, circumventing secondary structure issues inherent to shRNA oligonucleotides. The E2 shRNA library showed uniform distribution (CV 37.9%, AUC 0.68) with <0.04% wildtype remnants and >60% functional knockdown of GFP.
results.evaluation: Claims C70-C72 demonstrate successful shRNA synthesis through gel electrophoresis and Sanger sequencing. Functional validation (C74) shows >60% GFP reduction. NGS analysis (C75) confirms uniform distribution with metrics comparable to gRNA libraries. The Bsu36I digest control (C76, R²=0.9687) demonstrates that template removal doesn't affect distribution. This establishes 3Cs versatility beyond gRNA applications (C73, C77).

results.result: A TGW library with theoretical diversity of 7.3×10¹⁰ targeting 1.65×10⁷ genomic sites was generated and applied to doxorubicin resistance screening. Despite low experimental reproducibility (0.004%), 4,232 overlapping gRNAs were identified, validated, and mapped to coding genes including CysLTR2, whose chemical inhibition reversed doxorubicin resistance.
results.evaluation: The TGW library generation is well-documented (C22-C24, C81-C84) with uniform distribution (CV 0.26%, AUC 0.52). However, the doxorubicin screen has critically low reproducibility (0.004%, C87), though Spearman/Pearson correlations >0.75 (C88) suggest some consistency. The CysLTR2 validation (C92-C93) provides strong mechanistic support for one hit, but the low reproducibility and reliance on a validation screen (C89) raise concerns about false positives. The result demonstrates technical feasibility but requires more rigorous validation.

results.result: Computational analysis of doxorubicin resistance hits identified 192 coding and 222 noncoding gRNA targets (allowing ≤2 mismatches). Molecular signature analysis revealed enrichment for UV_RESPONSE_VIA_ERCC3 genes (25/178 coding hits, p=6.11E-17) and transcription factor targets (FOXO4, KLF1, NFAT) among noncoding hits, with 52.7% of noncoding hits lacking annotation.
results.evaluation: The computational mapping (C94-C95) and molecular signature analyses (C100, C106) are methodologically sound with significant p-values. The ERCC3 connection to doxorubicin resistance is supported by literature (C101-C102). However, the analysis relies on the reference genome (GRCh38.86) which may differ from hTERT-RPE1 cells, and allows up to 2 mismatches which increases false positive risk. The large fraction of unannotated noncoding hits (C105) and reliance on adjacent genes for analysis limits interpretability. The authors acknowledge these limitations (C126-C128).

results.result: An optimized TGW (oTGW) library was developed by truncating gRNAs to 17 nt, reducing diversity 50-fold to 1.5×10⁹ while maintaining identical genomic target coverage (1.65×10⁷ sites). Three oTGW libraries showed uniform distribution (AUC ≤0.54) with 0.2% wildtype remnants.
results.evaluation: The oTGW design rationale is supported by prior work on truncated gRNAs (C108). The diversity reduction calculation (C109-C110) is mathematically sound. NGS characterization of three independent libraries (C112-C113) demonstrates consistent quality metrics comparable to other 3Cs libraries. The claim of being "first of their kind" (C114) is reasonable given the scale and approach, though the potential impact remains to be demonstrated through functional screens.

results.result: The 3Cs technology offers unique advantages including applicability to all f1-origin plasmids, elimination of PCR amplification and dual oligonucleotides, low error rate (0.0015% mutations from T7 polymerase), and near-complete wildtype removal via placeholder sequences.
results.evaluation: These technical features are well-supported by the experimental data throughout the manuscript. The f1-origin applicability (C115) is demonstrated across multiple plasmid types. PCR elimination (C116) is inherent to the method design. The T7 polymerase error rate (C117) is supported by citation and calculation. Wildtype removal (C118) is consistently demonstrated across all libraries with NGS quantification showing <0.3% remnants.

results.result: Time-dependent analysis of the DUB screen revealed increased phenotype resolution for negative regulators over time, consistent with p53-mediated G1 arrest effects. DNA damage-associated DUBs (COPS6, USP7) are proposed as p53 alternatives for controlling DNA damage-induced cell cycle arrest in CRISPR screens.
results.evaluation: The time-dependent observations (C58) are supported by data comparing day 11 and day 21 timepoints. The interpretation is grounded in cited literature on p53-mediated CRISPR effects (C56) and prior work on USP28 (C120) and COPS6/USP7 (C121). The proposal to use DNA damage-associated DUBs as controls (C122) is a logical inference from the data and literature, though it requires prospective validation. The asymmetric resolution between positive and negative phenotypes (C59) is explained by prior work.

results.result: The authors discuss future applications of 3Cs to rAAV and adenoviral systems, acknowledge limitations of fully randomized libraries (requiring 2.2×10¹⁴ cells for 20N coverage), and recognize computational challenges including sensitivity to incorrect cut site calling and genome reference mismatches.
results.evaluation: The future applications (C119) are reasonable extrapolations given the method's generality. The mathematical analysis of fully randomized library limitations (C123-C125) is correct and highlights practical constraints. The acknowledged computational limitations (C126-C128) demonstrate appropriate scientific rigor. The proposed workflow using oTGW for discovery followed by targeted validation (C129-C130) is a logical experimental strategy, though speculative.

results.result: Background context establishes that conventional CRISPR library generation methods are labor-intensive, require PCR amplification and cloning, introduce sequence bias that affects library quality, while CRISPR/Cas has become the gold standard for functional genomics. Kunkel mutagenesis using M13 phage has been successful for phage display applications.
results.evaluation: These background claims (C1-C2, C9-C13) are well-supported by multiple citations to established literature. The characterization of M13 phage biology (C14) and Kunkel mutagenesis (C15-C17) is accurate and appropriately cited. These claims provide necessary context for understanding the motivation and novelty of the 3Cs approach but do not constitute original findings of this manuscript.
